speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the absence of the Minister of Justice I should like to direct this question to the Prime Minister. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: FAILURE TO EXECUTE WARRANT FOR ARREST OF HAL BANKS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I do not know his whereabouts, but inquiries are being made and it is hoped that a statement can be made tomorrow.

subtopic: FAILURE TO EXECUTE WARRANT FOR ARREST OF HAL BANKS
speechtext:
I see the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice is now present, so may I direct this supplementary question to him. Is the Prime Minister or the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice not somewhat surprised that neither he nor his officials in the Department of Justice are aware of Banks' whereabouts? I have been advised by Montreal radio station CKGM, and in particular by Ed Murphy,
a radio commentator, that Hal Banks up to yesterday, and probably today, was apparently at Higgins beach, Scarborough, main post office, Higgins beach, U.S.A. If that information is correct, what is the Department of Justice intending to do about it? Do they intend to institute extradition proceedings?

subtopic: FAILURE TO EXECUTE WARRANT FOR ARREST OF HAL BANKS

As I said yesterday, I have asked for a full statement on this from the department, and I would expect that a more complete statement will be available when the minister returns tomorrow.

subtopic: FAILURE TO EXECUTE WARRANT FOR ARREST OF HAL BANKS
speechtext: A further supplementary question. Do I take it from the parliamentary secretary that he or the officials of the Department of Justice are aware of Hal Banks' whereabouts, but because of legal procedure or for other reasons they do not intend to do anything immediately with regard to making an early arrest?

speechtext:
should like to address a question to the Secre-

tary of State for External Affairs. The other day the minister informed the house that the United Nations secretary general had received a reply from the government of Turkey respecting the build-up of forces on Cyprus-

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Greece.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I am sorry-from Greece, but had received no reply from the government of Turkey. He also said a reply had just come in from the government of Cyprus but he had not had time to read it. Can the minister give us some idea of the contents of that message and say whether it is true that Archbishop Makarios has informed the United Nations that the present build-up of men and war materiel will continue despite the request from the secretary general that it should be discontinued?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: A reply from the head of the government of Cyprus was received by the secretary general, and I was so advised. I have also been advised that it does not meet with the satisfaction of the secretary general, who has communicated in turn with the head of the government of Cyprus. The reply of the archbishop is not consistent with the declaration made by the prime minister of Greece. There has been a reply as well from the prime minister of Turkey, and a statement is expected by the secretary general today or tomorrow, I believe.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Would the secretary of state tell us whether it is correct that the archbishop's message indicated that the government of Cyprus intends to continue the buildup of both men and materiel on the island?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: The statement of the archbishop was to the effect that in the absence of an assurance of no invasion it was necessary for the government of Cyprus to take means to protect itself. As I say, the secretary general of the United Nations has communicated directly with the government of Cyprus with regard to this reply.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Is it being made clear to the archbishop that the presence of the United Nations force on the island is the very assurance for which he is asking?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: That has been made clear by the secretary general and, I may say, by Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Some weeks ago it was suggested by members of the opposition that rules should be promulgated which would empower

the United Nations force in Cyprus to prevent what has actually occurred since, namely incursions by troops from outside the country. Is it now a fact that belatedly the United Nations secretary general has made new rules in this connection?
If so, what is the nature thereof, and will these rules enable our forces as part of the United Nations force to keep out those who would surreptitiously find their way into Cyprus and thereby aggravate the already perilous situation in that island?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the authority of the force does not extend to the right to prevent the ingress of arms or men from outside. The government of Cyprus asserts that this is a right that belongs to it as the duly constituted authority. The view of the United Nations commander and the strong view of the participating governments, is that the terms of reference laid down in accordance with the security council resolution provide for the free movement of the United Nations troops, and that there should be no denial of access of those troops to any area on the island for the purpose of discharging their functions. In a communication I sent quite recently to the secretary general I indicated that I thought this point ought to be taken up very strongly through the commander, and that is now being done.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Is it then a fact that Archbishop Makarios places himself in the position of taking the stand that the United Nations forces are not allowed to do anything to prevent incursions from outside? If it is, the United Nations force is completely powerless, and the situation will become worse and worse as Makarios becomes more and more defiant of the United Nations.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
My right hon. friend will understand, I am sure, that I have a responsibility at the moment which I wish to discharge. Bearing in mind the important observation he has made, I do not want to say anything that is going to cause difficulty. However, I will say I am firmly of the view, as are the other participating governments in the force, and the commander and the secretary general, and as both the prime minister of Greece and the prime minister of Britain confirmed yesterday, that but for the presence of the United Nations force in Cyprus the situation would be much worse. Great as the difficulties are, we must continue to support the presence of that force, notwithstanding the position taken by particular authorities. If the United Nations force
Inquiries of the Ministry is not able to discharge its responsibilities this will be serious not only for Cyprus but also for NATO, and as serious for the United Nations and for the ultimate role that we hope it will play in situations like this in the future in other places.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, all of which general observation I agree with, but is it not most serious when the United Nations force in that country is treated with contemptuous and cavalier disregard by Makarios? What does the minister say?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: My right hon. friend knows that my reaction would be as his, but I do not want to say anything that is going to complicate what is now being done on that island to deal with this very kind of situation, and I am sure my right hon. friend appreciates that.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am sure all hon. members will agree with the general statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but may I ask him if it is not time that the United Nations made it clear to Archbishop Makarios that the time has come for him to start cooperating with the United Nations peace keeping force rather than using it as a pawn for his own purposes?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the time has come for all elements from the involved countries, for the government of Cyprus, and for both communities there, and for other outside nations, to co-operate in trying to bring about some solution to this difficult problem and in trying to bring about peace as a condition precedent to that solution.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a supplementary question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In answering a question put to him the minister made a statement concerning the United Nations forces in which we take an active participation and which contributed and still contribute to peace keeping activities on Cyprus. My question is this: How is it that we hear rumours here and there to the effect that our forces are absolutely useless on Cyprus? Some months ago the minister himself stated that our troops would be there for three months. The three months have gone by and, today, we are facing exactly the same problem as we did three months ago, and I

Inquiries of the Ministry should like to hear the minister tell the house what is actually the part played by our Canadian soldiers on the island of Cyprus, that is what do they do to maintain peace on that island?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, our Canadian troops are members of the United Nations forces and they are there in order to attempt to contribute to peace-

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: To attempt.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: -to attempt to contribute to peace. That is all they can do, and I do not think there could be a nobler task.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-STEPS TO RESOLVE SEAMEN'S STRIKE

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-STEPS TO RESOLVE SEAMEN'S STRIKE

At the same time it is the wish and hope of the government and, I am sure, of all hon. members that the benefits of this legislation should be available to students in all parts of Canada for the next academic year. Hon. members will appreciate that this poses a particular difficulty in so far as the Yukon is concerned where, as the hon. member for Yukon knows perhaps better than any of us, writs were issued on July 10 calling for an election. The election will be held on September 8. It is my under-

standing that the writs will not be returnable until October 16 and that the first meeting of the council will probably be called for early November.
If we were to insist that the commissioner of the Yukon consult with the council or, for that matter, with the advisory committee on finance before any action is taken, it would mean that no appropriate authority could be designated and therefore no loans could be granted to students in the territory in time for the next academic year. This is the case because until the elections have been held and the writs returned there will be no council and no advisory committee with whom the commissioner could consult.
In the case of the Northwest Territories I understand that the next meeting of the council will be held in November. It might be possible, I suppose, to call a special meeting some time in August, but I do not know whether this would be convenient for the members of the council or whether they would feel it was necessary to do so.
In these circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I understand that the hon. member for Yukon would be willing, provided the government first of all withdraws its amendment, to withdraw the subamendment so the government may move a new amendment which would take into account the points about consultation which were raised by the hon. member and by other hon. members, and which at the same time would meet the legal points which have been of concern to the government. If this course is followed it would permit action to be taken this year, of necessity without consultation in so far as the Yukon is concerned this year but it would provide for consultation in the future.

Mr. Chairman, with reference to clause 4 which concerns the interest free

Loans to Students
and repayment period, I am completely in agreement with the principle of the bill but I am concerned with the method to be used in establishing need for a loan, in view of the fact that loans are interest free to a student. While the bill states that authority for granting loans shall be designated by the lieutenant governor in any province, it does not clearly define those who may be eligible for loans. This will invariably lead to discrimination among the provinces, for the definition of the word "need" may be entirely different among the provinces of Canada. This could result in loans being made in one province while loans are denied citizens of similar means in other provinces.
In my opinion under this legislation it would appear unnecessary for anyone regardless of means to pay each year for his children's education. For example, a man may be worth $100,000 and have it invested in securities or mortgages at a rate of 6 per cent for a five year period, therefore his money would not be readily available. In these circumstances his son would be justified in borrowing up to $5,000 over a period of five years to help pay for his education, and under the bill this money is interest free. At the end of the five year period plus six months the parent could sell his securities which had been paying him 6 per cent and then repay his son's loan. During this period the $5,000 earned $1,500 interest not compounded. I have not figured it out, but at compound interest I believe the sum would be in excess of $2,000.
It is for this reason, as I have stated earlier, that every parent will avail himself of the opportunity to secure $5,000 in interest free money if he has a child going to college. I would ask the minister, is this the intention of this legislation? If so, it will have more far reaching effect than was originally anticipated. If this rule does not apply then it is discriminatory against many Canadians, since the basis of need will not have been established. I should like to have the minister's interpretation of the point I have raised. In other words, will there be a means test under which these loans will be made available so they will be distributed fairly and equitably right across Canada?

tical way was to have the sections of this act which deal with the students themselves and their needs dealt with by provincial bodies who have been doing this same work in some cases for many years.
As to the fear of the hon. member that people may take advantage of these provisions; that people who do not really need the money will borrow it, interest free, and then possibly lend it to their parents, or in other words beat the game in one way or another, I can only say that I do not think the great majority of the people it is proposed to help to obtain higher education in one form or another are the kind of people who will deliberately set out to evade what is the clear intention of this bill. There may be individual cases where this will happen. If there are many of them, I suppose the act will be brought into question and amendments will be necessary. But on the advice of the provincial officials who have helped prepare this bill it is proposed to leave the criteria to the authorities in each province to work out. In most cases they have done so already.

Now that we have come to clause 7 I wonder whether I might be permitted to answer some questions that the hon. member for Ontario raised the other day. He has been very patient, for which I am grateful, although not so much for his questions as for his patience. He first of all asked what was meant by the term "vocational equivalent of a university education". I think the point is that loans would be available for students who are taking certain vocational training programs which require, like universities a high school diploma as a prerequisite for enrolment. Those students taking courses which the federal government now supports under program No. 2 of the vocational training agreements would be eligible in the provinces, if the provinces so decide. In short, it will be up to each province to determine which post-secondary institutions will be designated.
The next question was whether the requirement that a student must be studying at a post-secondary school level would work an injustice in the case, for example, of Ontario students who take grade 13 in high school and thus cannot qualify for a loan, when in some provinces grade 13 is taken at university thereby entitling such grade 13 students to qualify for a loan. I do not think there is any great injustice. Ontario students taking grade 13 at high school do not have to pay tuition fees so any injustice there may be, would be quite minor. They do not have to pay tuition fees. Similar students in another province taking grade 13 at university do have to pay tuition fees and their financial need is there-

fore greater. In any case there appears to be a trend toward evening out these requirements. I must say, however, as I have said before, that it is not the intention to have uniform standards across the country, and if this provision tends to promote some mobility amongst students in Canada I think it may be helpful.
The next question was: Will the loan plan cause an increase in enrolment and, if so, how much? I would hope and believe that there will be some increase in enrolment as full time students on the part of many who are now taking night courses and others who are financially unable to afford a university education at the present time. It is not possible, however, to forecast the magnitude of the increase in enrolment which this legislation may bring about.
The next question was: What happens to a student who drops out during a university year and then cannot find work immediately? Who is responsible for repaying the loan? That was the question asked by the hon. member for Lapointe a minute ago. As I indicated, we do not expect this will be a common experience since the loans are to be made to people who have demonstrated that they possess satisfactory scholastic standards. However there may be some drop-outs of this kind, and I think each case will have to be dealt with on its own merits and in the light of the regulations.

Following our meeting today with Hon. Walter Gordon, Minister of Finance, Hon. Maurice Lamon-tagne, Secretary of State, and Mr. Jean-Charles Cantin, parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport, we want to explain once again why we are opposing federal loans.
We feel that Bill No. C-110 runs directly counter to provincial jurisdiction as far as education is concerned. It does not seem in any way acceptable that the federal government should interfere in a field where planning, decisions and amounts of money granted are the exclusive right of the provincial authorities; we cannot consider as worthy the argument that the federal government has the right, because it has the fiscal autonomy, to use in its own way the money received from taxpayers; such an action becomes unconstitutional as soon as it affects the field of education.

The autonomy of the provinces will be all the more respected if we, ourselves, refuse to yield in that field. I was not reading a press release but a telegram addressed by the premier of the province of Quebec to the Minister of Finance and I had mentioned it before. I shall start over again, then:
Hon. Walter Gordon, Minister of Finance, House
of Commons, Ottawa, Ont.

Loans to Students
Under section 12 of Bill No. C-110, every provincial government is free to withdraw from the application of the federal legislation concerning student loans by informing the Minister of Finance of Canada that a similar program will be set up in the province and that no authority will be designated in that province for the purpose of the federal legislation. Since such notice must be given within 30 days of the passage of that act, the Quebec government informs you this very day that it intends to withdraw from the federal program of student loans as soon as the act designed to establish such program will be ratified. As you know, the province of Quebec already has a provincial loan program.
Therefore, we demand-
And this is the interesting part of it.
Therefore, we demand the alternative payment provided under paragraph 2, section 12 of Bill No. C-110.
Allow me now to digress and depart from the telegram. The Quebec premier proves that he has never understood that the Quebec people are asking for provincial autonomy in the educational field and for the respect of constitutional rights.
We do not want the government to collect taxes and then hand over part of it to the provincial government so that it may use that money for educational purposes. This is not what we want. We have always objected to that.
Before and during the last provincial electoral campaign, the premier said: We want Quebec to control its sources of revenue, so that it can spend that money as it sees fit, in the field of education, instead of allowing the federal government to collect taxes and then to give handouts to Quebec so that it is able to apply that money to education.
The premier should have understand that a long time ago. Now Mr. Lesage is trying to justify himself:
Since the amount involved represents only a very small sum-
One per cent of the personal income tax.
-we shall accept, for the time being, the payment of a financial equivalent-
Because it represents the amount, an amount of about $700,000.
The premier prefers an equivalent.
The students have taught him quite a lesson in that field, because whatever the amount suggested, be it $700,000 or $5 million, it is the principle rather than the money which counts. The Minister of Finance did not understand that and the Quebec premier indicates now that he did not understand it either. Besides, the Quebec university students, when they wrote to the Minister of Finance letters which were read earlier in

the house, said: It is not a matter of $700,000, but a matter of principle. Let it be respected. For $700,000 shall we sell down the river rights granted by the Canadian constitution in 1867? For $700,000 are we going to sell, to the federal government, our rights in the field of education?
The students have well understood it, they who are primarily concerned, who need it most. Why do they object? They object to the fact that this represents a violation of the constitution.
Well, the Quebec premier did not understand that and added, and I am quoting his last words:
We will accept for the time being an equivalent financial payment provided that this equivalent payment is applied in the case of federal programs to which Quebec does not see fit to participate-
Meanwhile, the Quebec premier accepts Ottawa's grants in the field of education. But we have always claimed the right to a tax deduction or abatement. It would represent perhaps one tenth or two tenths of 1 per cent.
Whatever it may be, there is a principle involved; if we forsake the principle in return for a sum of $700,000, as many others have mentioned, will we forsake it for $3,000,000? Where will we draw the line?
Mr. Chairman, compensation payments have been mentioned; well, compensation payments have never been accepted in the province of Quebec. It would be the first time. It will be recalled that the province of Quebec had not accepted direct grants to Quebec universities nor had it accepted compensation payments.
What has Quebec accepted? It has accepted to collect 1 to 2 per cent of personal income tax. Let Quebec collect that amount and distribute it in grants to universities and the principle, the rights of Quebec in the field of education, the constitution and the autonomy of the province in the field of education would be safeguarded.
That is what we want to safeguard: the principle involved. We are asked to sacrifice a matter of principle when a small amount is involved, whereas the students themselves are ready to do without those subventions in order to safeguard a principle.
I wonder if the Minister of Finance would not be prepared to safeguard the matter of principle so as not to fan the flames of dissatisfaction, to move an amendment and certify that Quebec could benefit from a tax rebate, which it would collect itself, a rebate equivalent to the amount that would now be paid in subsidies. That would be the equivalent of two tenths of 1 per cent.

I understand that might complicate matters, but this is a bilingual country and bilingualism complicates matters, there is no doubt about that. We live in a country where it is said all the time that Quebec is not a province like the others, but when the time comes to deal with Quebec, it is treated like the others.
We do not ask more than the other provinces, we do not ask less, but we ask that when acts affecting the rights of the province of Quebec are drafted, the principle not the amount to be given back to the province of Quebec be taken into account-we are ready to accept a tax rebate equivalent to the amount the other provinces would receive. We do not want more, but not less either than what the other provinces will get. On the other hand, we want the principle to be respected, we want that when it is said that the province of Quebec is not a province like the others, everybody understands that it is because that province keeps a watchful eye on the rights belonging to it under the constitution, while the other provinces are not doing so.
The Minister of Finance is able, since he has three experts at his beck and call, to find a formula. Instead of having alternative payments, amounts paid out of charity by Ottawa to the province of Quebec, let Quebec collect funds from its own income sources. This can be compensated by two tenths of 1 per cent.
At present, I doubt that it is two tenths of 1 per cent. I figure that under subsection 2- as if often happens with the Minister of Finance-that such a number must be multiplied by such a coefficient, then the residue must be divided by such a number in relation to another one while the proper product is subtracted, allowance being made for the amount in such a paragraph.
There is an algebra problem there; I examined it thoroughly and I will show it to the minister tonight. It is a silly problem as it is a mix-up of loaned amounts, the bases of which have no foundation at all. Students who are taking courses are mixed up with the number of those who are not taking courses. It reminds me of the problem where you have 10 farmers having 20 cows each; you ask someone to multiply the number of feet, to divide by the number of ears and then to give you the number of gallons of milk you will get at the end of the year.
Mr. Chairman, do the division, the multiplication and the subtraction; do all that and you will find out that there is no sense in it.

I agree entirely, and probably this is the only time in many years, with the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, that the Bell Telephone Company should be considered as a

crown corporation. The reason for this is the inherent faults that lie in monopoly control. This corporation has not produced results, so far as the consumers are concerned, that were produced so far as the shareholders are concerned.
I think it is shocking when one looks at some of the problems we have had, Mr. Chairman. The last speaker mentioned that the Minister of Finance hoped many more of our corporations would be profit making, and that they would be Canadian. The long list of corporate directors of the Bell Telephone Company that was put on the record certainly reads like a who's who of the industrial, corporate and stockbroking world of Canada. One could come to the conclusion that it might not only be United States domination that is dangerous, but any type of monopoly control in Canada may be dangerous and may be detrimental to the operation of any corporation.
Now, one hon. member has mentioned the fact that crown corporations are not always a success. I do not believe he was really talking about crown corporations because the federal government has many of them that are successful. Many of them are operating in a field in which they could not operate at all and provide a service if they were not crown corporations and were not subsidized to some extent. This is true, of course, in the transportation field. After looking over the list the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm put on Hansard today, I think it will be easy to come to the conclusion that monopoly control of any segment of our economy cannot be anything but detrimental to the nation. If we are going to allow a continuation of this huge monopoly in the field of communication, then in my opinion we are going to have to allow the members of parliament to have a better opportunity of scrutinizing the operations of that company.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
The Bell Telephone Company was set up under a federal charter which would allow it to operate in the whole field of communications in Canada. There were certain limitations put on it. I believe that, since it has a federal charter, any attempt to change the structure of the company would have to take place in the federal parliament and not in a provincial jurisdiction.
This raises an interesting problem. This company has been before us a number of times. It was here in 1886 for incorporation. It was here in 1882 to get a declaration of powers; in 1884 to get its capital increased. It returned in 1892 to have the capital increased and authority granted for a bond issue.
It came again in 1894 and had its capital increased, and also at that time the arrangement regarding the six months rate allowance was covered. This meant it would have the right where a person had bad credit to ask for an advance of six months expected payment. It came again in 1906 and once more increased its capital. It came in 1920 for a bond issue increasing its capital, and in 1948, as I understand it, with a submission to a royal commission. Again in 1957 there was another inquiry, and now the company returns seeking five additional directors.
Having listened to the list of directors supplied to the committee can anyone suggest any good reason why they would want to add five more, and where they would get five more when they are already overlapping so many other companies? Is there any company in Canada with which Bell Telephone has not a close relation? Having listened to the list supplied by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm I would think they have not missed anything. If they are seeking additional directors this can only mean they are going to want money from outside Canada, and they will be asking for international control rather than monopoly control of capital in Canada. I may say I also think they have government control because Mr. Bob Winters was not appointed to the directorate of that company simply because he was an engineer. The reason for his appointment is because he represents the Liberal government.
I am opposed to Bell Telephone for a very simple reason. They have no heart. They will not give any consideration to any representation made to them. They will not give any consideration to the individual who uses their telephones. They are autocratic in their control and bureaucratic in their operation, and

it is a fact that they make a huge amount of money. Under these circumstances how could they lose money? How could they not have a successful operation?
Since I last spoke on this matter I have received a number of letters and I would like to mention a number of problems raised in them before I move an amendment. The first problem is one which I am sure has been met by all members of parliament, and is one not confined strictly to the Bell Telephone Company. It is one sometimes made against the telephone company I use, the Northern Telephone Company, servicing northern Quebec and northern Ontario.
When a person moves from one residence to another and has his telephone connected in his new residence there is a $6 buzzing-in charge, even though the telephone is sitting there and all that has to be done is press a switch in the telephone office to connect the service. If the telephone had to be moved from one room to another, if a service call had to be made at the new residence, then this charge could be legitimate. At present this is an unreasonable charge for which the consumer receives no benefit whatsoever and for which there is no operational cost to the company. I believe we should have some way of conveying to the company that this buzzing-in charge is not really legitimate.
Another complaint concerns the number of times a customer is called and asked if he wishes to instal a fancy, pastel coloured telephone, for which there is an $11 charge. In fact a great deal of annoyance is given to a resident who does not comply with the request the first time it is made. I remember one incident in this connection when I went into the telephone office in Thessalon to make a long distance call. This was at the time of the discovery of uranium at Blind River and I used to find it more convenient to go to the next town to place calls. The girl operating the exchange there had a number of pastel coloured telephones on the counter. I asked her how much they were worth and she said I could have one for $11. I handed out $11 and was about to take one of these phones from the counter when she told me, "You cannot take it; there is an installation charge." I contend that that $11 charge by the Northern Telephone Company is simply for the sealed casing covering the instrument, and not the instrument itself, and because telephone companies have a monopoly they can charge this amount.
Another complaint concerns billing charges. If you make a complaint in Ottawa nobody

in the Ottawa office can do anything about it because the billing is done by I.B.M. in Montreal and the local office manager has to get in touch with Montreal.
I have one letter here concerning a bill that was overdue and I would like to read part of it. It was sent to me from St. Catharines, Ontario, and is dated July 10. It reads:
If you are collecting evidence to support your case, here is an instance just two weeks old.
A young woman running a store in this city has been forced to pay a "deposit'' of $150 as "assurance" of payment against any future monthly bill. When I say "forced to pay" $150 as security, I mean just that, forced to pay, as she was informed that if that sum was not paid by noon on a certain date (two day's notice) her phone would be disconnected.
Her phone bill for the month had been received only three days before and payment of this-$138 -was also demanded immediately. There were no arrears in payment.
The lady requested me to intercede on her behalf so that the demand for the $150 be withdrawn, but the person I saw at the telephone office refused to consider the request and later that day he phoned the woman to say that he would not even accept a certified cheque-it had to be cash-or the phone would be disconnected at 12 o'clock noon, that day. This is not service, it is tyranny.
The service referred to has been in use for six years. Last year, two cheques were returned marked "N.S.F." but on notification by the telephone company both cheques were immediately honoured. These two unfortunate instances are admitted.
However, during my interview I was told that the service had been withdrawn and the phone disconnected twice in 1963.
I said I had not been informed about that and requested my interviewer to write me stating these facts. He refused to do so and when I asked for the dates of the disconnections he said he could not give them to me as I was not the subscriber concerned-

Mr. Chairman, when the committee adjourned at five o'clock I was speaking on clause 12 and not on clause 11. I was trying to explain the famous algebraic calculation given in paragraph 2 of clause 12. Here is how the alternative payments are worked out:
An alternative amount for a province for any loan year is the amount, as determined by the minister after consultation with the dominion statistician, obtained by (a) multiplying
(i) the aggregate of all amounts paid by the minister in that loan year to banks pursuant to sections 6, 7, 8 and 9 in respect of guaranteed student loans-

Well, Mr. Chairman, I personally made the calculation. I know that the minister has three assistants before him who are undoubtedly good at algebra. If they would be kind enough to take note on a piece of paper of the data of the problem which I will submit to them, they will find that it makes no sense at all.
In (a) (i), there is:
The aggregate of all amounts paid by the minister in that loan year to banks pursuant to sections 6, 7, 8 and 9-
According to that clause 6, we have the interest paid by the minister during one year.
Then, if you wish, we could represent by a capital letter "A" the interest paid on the loans throughout Canada and we will represent by a small letter "a" the interest paid in one province only during one year.
Now, let us look at clause 7. These are the amounts which are not repaid but which, as a result of the minister's guarantee, the government is obliged to pay. Then, with a capital "B" we represent the losses sustained throughout Canada as a result of the guarantee, and with a small "b" we represent the losses sustained in a single province.
Now, clause 8 which is the third expenditure mentioned in clause 12 and which deals with the loss incurred as a result of the death of the borrower. Then with a capital "C" we represent the amounts paid, as a result of those deaths throughout Canada, and with a small "c" the amounts paid, as a result of those deaths, in a single province.

We now come to subparagraph (ii):
(A) the estimated number of persons in that province that, on the first day of that loan year, have attained eighteen years of age and have not attained twenty-five years of age.
Consequently, we will use a capital letter "E" to represent a group of people dispersed throughout Canada, and a small letter "e" to indicate a group confined to a single province.
That number has to be multiplied, that is, divided-since we take the coefficient-by the estimated number of persons in provinces where the appropriate authorities have issued or caused to be issued certificates of eligibility. Then, you have all the data of the problem. Mr. Chairman, that proves my point. This is extremely complicated. Besides, I reduced the data to the simplest expression and nevertheless, it is still complicated, and very few will be able to understand.
I was trying all this time to give as an example the amount I figured. This equation is impossible and mathematically incorrect. I shall now apply the equivalent figures to every letter I used. As a matter of course, "A" is the interest paid during the year under section 6. Therefore, 6 per cent of $40 million is $2.4 million. If approximately 30 per cent is applied to the province of Quebec, the letter "a" represents $720,000. If under section 7, "B", that is, the loss incurred through the guarantee, for instance, 7 per cent will amount to $8 million for the whole country and the letter "b", $2.4 million for the province of Quebec. If we represent the losses sustained as a result of death by a 3 per cent average, we shall have as value, for capital "C", $1,200,000 and about $360,000 for small "c". If we take capital "D" to represent the collection fees of half of 1 per cent for the whole of Canada, namely $200,000, the small "d" will equal $60,000.
Capital "E" represents the number of young people in Canada between the ages of 17 and 25 according to the Canadian statistics, therefore they would be about 1,500,000 and for the province of Quebec only, small "e", about 450,000.
Capital "F" would be equivalent to 210,000. This is what the minister indicated for the whole country, therefore small "f" would equal 60,000 for the province of Quebec only. Capital "G" equals 0; since it will not recover

the interest paid by the minister on the loans. The same for small "g".
As to capital "H", there is perhaps a 5 per cent recovery on the amounts guaranteed by the government, that is $2 million; and small "h" equals $600,000. Capital "J" and capital "K" equal 0; and small "j" and "k" would equal 0, because there is no possible revenue therein. This means that, if we insert figures into the equation I made just now, it would be equal to capital "A", plus capital "B", plus capital "C", plus capital "D", making up a total of $11,800,000, minus capital "G", plus capital "H", plus capital "J", plus capital "K", which makes $2 million; the total therefore would be $9,800,000. We therefore have to multiply by "e/f", which would give us 450,000, divided by 60,000, which makes 9, giving a total of $85 million.
Now we must substract, under paragraph (b), the sums a + b + c + d-that is $720,000, $2,400,000, $360,000 and $60,000 respectively, which makes a total of $3,540,000 and from which g + h -f j + k, that is $60,000, are subtracted, making $2,940,000, which must in its turn be subtracted from $85,000,000, which means that the answer to or solution of the equation would be $82,060,000, based on the figures given by the minister in the preceding algebraic equation.
The above equation means that the federal government should give Quebec, if that province accepts alternative payments, an amount of $82,060,000 on a total of $40 million for the whole of Canada, from which the Minister of Finance wants the students to benefit.
Mr. Chairman, you will agree with me that this does not make sense. The federal government wants to earmark $40 million for 10 provinces, when under this legislation, it should remit $82,060,000 to the province of Quebec.
Unless the federal government should decide to make use of the Bank of Canada, that is the result we get, but why? Because the minister is all mixed up in his arithmetic, he makes you subtract interests paid to persons who died during the period the program was being carried out. That is multiplied by amounts collected in respect of the loans and divided by the number of students who are attending school and those who are not.
As I was saying before recess, it reminds me of the 10 farmers who had 20 heads of cattle; you multiply by four legs and divide by two ears to find out the number of gallons of milk you will get at the end of the year.

It is exactly the same kind of algebraic equation he is now trying to shove down our throats.
I submitted my figures and if the Minister of Finance wants to check them, he has them too and will compile them. I used these same figures to calculate the algebraic equation which is found in clause 12.
I think we should at least revise those figures and see if there was a mistake somewhere, if the minister is not miscalculating somewhere. The way he is proposing that bill does not make sense.
In any case, even if I succeeded in proving that this clause did not make sense, the matter of principle would remain. The federal government is not entitled to make alternative payments in the field of education. The province of Quebec is jealous of its rights and wants instead to have its own sources of revenue.
To this effect, I have an amendment to introduce and if the Minister of Finance is willing to listen-I apologize to the majority of my colleagues, because usually we always want to introduce our amendments both in French and in English, but unfortunately, I did not have time to have it translated, because this happened during the lunch hour and there was no time to type it out-but I shall have a French copy sent over to them.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve, that section 12 be amended by the addition of the following words at the end of paragraph (1), the period being replaced by a comma:
Or the minister must turn over to any province that so wishes, taxation rights on personal income equivalent to the alternative payment calculated as provided under paragraph (2).
Mr. Chairman, our amendment will not change anything in the wording of the bill; paragraph (1) will remain exactly as it now reads.
If a province prefers alternative payments, it will be able to accept them. If it would rather obtain a share of income out of personal income tax equivalent to the alternative payment, it could get it. We are not asking for more than the alternative payment; we are not asking for less. We are asking exactly the same amount. And then the constitution will at least be respected.
This is a procedure used on several occasions by previous governments when grants were given directly to universities in the province of Quebec; at that time, the Quebec premier refused them. Afterwards, agreement was reached between the Conservative government of the time headed by the present
Loans to Students
Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Quebec premier was then Mr. Sauve, I think. In fact, this is what was called the Diefenbaker-Sauve agreement. The principle was acceptable for grants to universities. In fact, it was one of the most appreciated formula; this government accepted it on other occasions. That is why we were surprised that this formula was not accepted at this time.
At any rate, if the Minister of Finance wants to introduce an amendment, we shall be glad to let him move it for us. This will take nothing from anyone and will give nothing to anyone. The only result being that the principle will be respected. The Minister of Finance knows that Quebec has always had its heart set on those principles and that we shall not hesitate to fight for them.
If the minister wishes, we are prepared to withdraw our amendment so as to give him the opportunity to introduce it himself.
I ask the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) who understands rather well the feelings of the Quebec people, to move the amendment, just as he did on other occasions. He could move the amendment, seconded by another autonomist who sometimes defends the interests of Quebec, namely the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay).
Then everybody will be glad to see that Bill No. C-110 was amended to please everyone.
I ask the Minister of Finance and all government members to accept this amendment, since it does not take anything away from anyone, it does not give anyone anything, except that the principles we want to safeguard, the principles of the constitution, will be respected. Then everyone will be satisfied and no one will have cause to complain.

That clause 12, paragraphs (1), (2), etc., with (i), (ii), etc. is more complicated than the algebraic problem submitted to us a little earlier by the hon. member for Lapointe. Clause 12 of Bill No. C-110 is a real algebraic problem that the Minister of Finance is not even able to solve. There are unknown quantities he cannot find. It is impossible to get a direct answer.
Will the students from the province of Quebec who will borrow money get the federal guarantee? That is what we want to know.
The Minister of Finance cannot answer us. Should he ask his officials who are seated in front of him at present, could they tell us whether the loans made under the present regulations in the province of Quebec would be guaranteed by the federal government or by the government of the province of Quebec? That is what we want to know. For should the province of Quebec guarantee the loans granted to students within that province, then the federal government would not have the right, constitutionally speaking, to collect a single cent in taxes in the province of Quebec.
That does not mean that we stand against those who support the plan as prepared or proposed. If other provinces wish to adopt it, let them do so. But people should stop saying in this house that Quebec citizens or the members from the province of Quebec, Liberals, Conservatives or others, are against that plan because they come from the province of Quebec.
We want the rights of the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta, British Columbia, just as the rights of the maritimes and of the province of Quebec, to be respected integrally and absolutely, especially as regards education.
The Minister of Finance is aware of the fact that education comes under the provinces and not under the House of Commons of Canada.

As it is, the central government at Ottawa infringes upon the rights of the provinces, even if we hear some hon. members like the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) say that only the province of Quebec is against Bill No. C-110 and more particularly against clause 12. It is not as much that we want to object to clause 12 as to the fact that the federal government interferes in the field of education in Canada. Education belongs to the provinces. The province of Quebec must be respected just like all the other provinces.
If the Minister of Finance continues to offer us problems like the one he is putting to us at this moment, by working out equalizations, compensations, by dividing, subtracting, multiplying without ever knowing where he is going, Mr. Chairman, we cannot accept the bill in such a form and substance.

First, I considered it was not up to me, as an humble member, to decide whether that amendment satisfied everybody and I felt I could not take it upon myself to commit my colleagues to it.
Then, the amendment proposed by the Minister of Justice only covered the form of procedure, whereas there is much more to the

bill inasmuch as it involves the very essence of civil law.
Mr. Chairman, I have followed with great interest all the discussions which took place in committee on this bill. Yesterday, speaking to the motion introduced by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), I think the Minister of Finance said something like this: "The purpose of this legislation is to mobilize financial resources to help students; it is a bank bill."
Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer to the five point program of the Liberal party in the last election campaign, in which it is stated in chapter 2 "that the Liberal party would introduce, for vocational training, a measure to establish a fund for student loans, these loans bearing interest only a year after the completion of studies."
Why is the government trying today to make us believe that this legislation is a banking measure?
Mr. Chairman, it will be alleged that the proposed legislation is based on section 95 of the Bank Act, which is chapter 12 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. I also know that the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance or to the Minister of Justice will quote a judgment passed by the privy council or the supreme court to point out that persons under age are allowed to carry out banking operations.
I respectfully submit that in the opinion of the highest judicial authorities, it is necessary to interpret the scope and nature of the action taken by those carrying out banking operations under subsection 1 of section 95.
But I respectfully submit that in this case it is not a banking operation nor a banking transaction. To transact from the civil point of view, it is necessary to take into consideration the legal capacity of persons transacting or dealing with the bank to secure a loan, in accordance with the objective of that legislation.
The Minister of Finance and more especially the Minister of Justice have been quite annoyed when members on this side of the house raised several legal questions about the study of this bill.
As shown on page 5789 of Hansard for July 21, 1964, the Minister of Justice stated the following:
As I said, Mr. Chairman, there is not much point in getting into technical, involved, legal argument.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that it behoves us all to examine the legal effect of the piece of legislation now before us. If legislators are entrusted with the passage 20220-3744

of this measure in accordance with the needs of the population, I believe that lawyers, not exclusively but specially, must scrutinize the bill, must examine its legal effect and the data relating thereto. That is why I intend to bring in an amendment respecting clause 15 of the bill in a moment.

If nobody rises to refute the legal argumentation I am bringing forward, then I will conclude that you allow the very basis of provincial autonomy to be undermined for the benefit of a political party or to satisfy an election promise you made during the election campaign.
Clause 15 concerns an exclusively civil problem. This section deals with the legal capacity of citizens. Under this act, you consider that a person under age is of full age.
Now, I submit respectfully that we must face then an imperative provision of civil rights which fall within the jurisdiction of the province, according to sections 92 and 93 of the constitution.
I submit respectfully that the exclusive rights of provincial legislatures are defined in section 92 and specially in section 93 dealing with the property of civil rights.
I had the opportunity to study for quite a while, in co-operation with the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Marti-neau), the whole structure of the civil code and of the code of civil procedure of the province of Quebec. I am sure that the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) will quote, during the study of that section, the various points at issue.
However, I want to make it clear that I do not intervene to safeguard the civil law of the province of Quebec. If I do so, it is to protect the civil rights of the ten Canadian provinces.

I was saying, Mr. Chairman, that there is a legislation which is called pith and substance, that is colorated legislation. That is what the government is presenting, Mr. Chairman, because the courts decided they had to face the facts and the true implications of a piece of legislation, and not its form.
On the pretext of allowing banks to make loans to students, the people of Canada are offered a colorated piece of legislation, because the bill under consideration is primarily concerned with helping education and students. Besides, when he introduced this bill, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) was careful to mention that, in so doing, he was fulfilling part of the Liberal party platform.
Mr. Chairman, we are dealing in this case with a colorated piece of legislation, that is to say the federal government legislates in a field foreign to it, that is a field which belongs exclusively to the provinces, under the terms of section 92 of the British North America Act.
It was decided that in such a case the legislation should be declared unconstitutional. In the decisions of the privy council, "colorated legislation" is the name given to legislation which has been given a false look to have it fall in a different category from that to which it belongs.
If this is not colorated legislation, what is it then, Mr. Chairman?
We legislate for a definite purpose: help education and students-by means of a bill now under consideration-that is through credit that will be granted by the banks.
I wonder if during the last election campaign our learned friends opposite explained to the people the attraction of an amendment to the Bank Act. If this is banking legislation, why submit it to us under this guise? The government needed only to introduce an amendment to change the Bank Act.
There is a well known case, Attorney General of Canada v. attorney of Alberta. 1916, Appeal Cases, page 584, which I take the liberty of quoting to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). I hope he will ask his advisers to check this jurisprudence, which comes from the privy council.
The matter in that case consisted of a legislative measure that the province of Alberta

had brought forward in order to tax the banking institutions operating within the province. The case was even brought before the privy council, which ruled that banks were federal institutions and that, therefore, the provinces did not have that right. For this theory concerning the colorated legislation is reversible, that is, that it must apply to the federal as well as to the provincial field.
It is under such colorated legislation that this legislative measure brought forward by the attorney general for Alberta was ruled wholly illegal by the privy council.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we could quote also two other cases from the privy council, namely, the Reciprocal Insurance case, 1923, Appeal Cases, page 340, and another case, attorney general of Canada v. attorney general for Alberta, 1939, Appeal Cases, page 117.
I challenge the learned attorneys on the other side of the house. I have listened with great interest to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Cantin). His intervention was a little cold, a little uneasy, a little-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have a little private confab going on at this end.
The more I listen to the Minister of Public Works and his colleagues, the more they seem to confuse bills and loans. The whole bill is replete with the term "loan". A loan comports a promise to pay. I would suggest that the Minister of Public Works, whose emphasis on banking transactions does not bring him within any bank act or anything, has run afoul of the Bills of Exchange Act. I know the argument the minister may advance, but I would say that in so far as civil rights and contractual obligations are concerned with respect to any loan made under this or any other act, they are subject to the law of con-

tract and the civil rights of a province. I do not think there is any question in regard to that.
Therefore, we must look to the terms as to what is going to be done. Money is going to be borrowed. There will be an undertaking to repay. I put it to the minister that a promissory note is involved here, not only in the narrow sense but in the widest sense possible. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice may shake his head, but I think he sees the point I have in mind. We know what a promissory note is. Under the terms of the Bills of Exchange Act, chapter 15 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, a promissory note is an unconditional promise in writing which is made by one person to another- all the terms are satisfied so far-signed by the maker, engaging to pay on demand or at a fixed and determinable future time a sum certain in money to the order of a specified person or to bearer. I could also bring in the operation of sections 47, 48 and 186 of the Bills of Exchange Act which go to capacity to contract.
Now, we know for certain that a minor cannot sign a bill of exchange under the terms of this act, with the exception of enforcement by a holder in due course. But any bank knowing it is dealing with a minor is not a holder in due course. I know this is legal and technical, so the Minister of Industry had better pay attention. By section 186 all the conditions applying to bills of exchange and capacity to contract are applied to promissory notes.
It may be that this argument will be countered-and I am trying to meet the arguments ahead of time-by saying that because the crown has undertaken to indemnify the banks in the event of death, this is not an unconditional promise to pay. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that all the government has substituted here is a form of guaranteed payment, the same as though it had endorsed its name on the back of the note. Hon. gentlemen opposite who do not agree with me would have to argue that if a parent or relative or guardian were acting as endorser of a note, it would not be an unconditional promise to pay, and therefore not a note within the terms of the act.
Regulations under clause 13 as accepted by the committee prescribe the measures to be taken by the banks in the event of default and the procedure to be followed by the banks to recover the amount of the loan outstanding. The statement that a loan will not be collectible from the estate of the deceased

student who still owes money is a form of guarantee. It does not amount to an unconditional promise in writing to the bank. Remember, the promise is to the bank, and there are no conditions attached to the banks power to recover money lent; no disability imposed upon the bank as to its right to recover. Therefore I say this loan agreement is to be an unconditional promise in writing. Some people may suggest that because of the various undertakings the form will not be that of a promissory note.
Have hon. members seen the form of note under the arrangements for making a home improvement loan, or a note under section 88 of the Bank Act? It is a document almost a yard long, but still it is a promissory note. It does not matter. The promissory note is included within the entire document and one cannot get around it. It is there, and I suggest that by insisting this was loan legislation, strictly a financial matter, the government has merely become trapped deeper and deeper. They cannot have it both ways. It would have been better to have wiped out this clause entirely, because the banks, having taken security in the form of a note from an infant, will enforce it within the province. The infant defendant must raise the defence of being an infant, and we know that that is not an entire defence, so the burden is upon the student to prove that this was a form of promissory note for which he would not be liable. I would say that the chances of recovery would be 99,999 per cent and that the defence would not succeed.
I would suggest that the amendment put forward by my colleague from Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere placing liability for this type of loan strictly under provincial jurisdiction is merely declaratory and does not impose any rights or obligations, whereas this particular clause proposed by the government does, affecting also civil rights over which we have no authority; and therefore I claim that the clause is bad. I would certainly accept the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Dela-naudiere, it being merely declaratory.

Let me assure the hon. member for Lapointe that I shall be very happy to let him have the floor in a few minutes, when I finish my remarks It is precisely in my capacity of seconder of this motion that I want to intervene at this stage to support the amendment moved by that learned lawyer, the hon. member for Ber-thier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere.
I think that the government could have avoided many pitfalls if, instead of rather lackadaisically preparing the bill, it had followed the advice of such competent lawyers as my hon. friend, the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere.
The most striking part of the argument advanced by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, were his remarks concerning the legislation commonly called "coloured legislation" or "the pith and substance of the legislation".
Naturally, I listened with great attention to the Minister of Public Works. The more he progressed in his argument, the more I realize this was indeed "coloured legislation", in other words, legislation which is intended to look different from what it is in

Loans to Students
fact. I do not believe that the minister can seriously say this is mainly a banking legislation, and that the ends and intentions of this legislation concerning loans to students are only ancillary conclusions of this legislation, which would primarily be banking legislation.
This becomes apparent when we consider various points in this legislation and also when we analyse the presentation the Minister of Finance gave it in the first instance in introducing the resolution before the house, it was apparent when, two days ago, the bright parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pennell) also outlined the aims and the nature of this legislation.
In each intervention they both put forward the need for adopting this legislation in order to help students.
By any chance, has this resolution been introduced in order to help the banks? If the answer to my first question is in the affirmative and if the answer to my second question is in the negative, it is absolutely apparent that this is a legislation under colour-colour is an important word in the context-of being banking legislation, or else altogether different legislation. This is a legislation the nature of which mainly concerns public education and public teaching.
Mr. Chairman, if such is the case, under the constitution the federal government does not have the right to legislate in the matter on the basis of his ancillary powers, because they are simply reserved for cases concerning matters falling mainly within the competence of the federal government. Such is not the case. We have another proof of that if we look at the very title of this legislation-
An act to facilitate the making of loans to students.
Therefore, we must conclude that from a constitutional point of view, it is a matter concerning which the federal government has no right to legislate.
Second, we come to the point where it is also a legislation which transgresses the whole economy of our system and that goes also for my colleagues of all the other provinces, because there is not only the civil code of the province of Quebec, but also the basic principles of common law which stand as statutes all across Canada.
That is why we, as federal legislators, are quite at ease to deal with that, not only to defend the civil code of the province of

Quebec, but also to defend the merits of the common law applicable in all other regions of the country.
Mr. Chairman, we must therefore ask ourselves whether this clause concerns only the legal capacity or the minority of the contracting parties. Indeed, no other conclusion is possible, because clause 15 says:
A guaranteed student loan made by a bank to a borrower not of full age, and interest thereon other than interest payable under section 6, is recoverable by a bank from the borrower as though the borrower had been of full age at the time the loan was made.
It must then be ascertained what is meant by a person under age and for that, we must refer to section 246 of the civil code of the province of Quebec which reads as follows:
Persons of either sex remain in minority until they attain the full age of 21 years.
Well, what is the objective of this clause? It is deemed to contradict directly section 246 which provides that the condition of the minor remains till the age of 21 years, and this by a legislative text which is unconstitutional as far as this parliament's powers are concerned. They want to transform a person under age into a person of full age. Well, this condition of being under age under the civil rights of the province of Quebec entails many consequences, and clause 15 as worded contradicts all these consequences.
For the information of the Minister of Public Works, I could list the main sections of the civil code of the province of Quebec which are contradicted by this absolutely incongruous provision. You have, for instance, section 248 of the civil code which reads as follows:
The disabilities, the rights and privileges resulting from minority, the acts the minor may do and the suits he may bring, the cases in which he may demand to be relieved, the manner and time of making the demand, and other like questions, are determined in the third book of the present code, and in the code of civil procedure.
There is a whole series of basic sections of our civil code which are violated by these explicit provisions. These are sections 304, 643, 763, 831, 833, 907, 938, 1001s, 1267, 1707, 2030, 2031, 2086, 2114, 2147b, 2157b, 2232, 2243, 2269; they are all in the civil code as well as sections 78, 174, 1177, 1209, 1263 of the civil procedure code. Those are basic sections which all concern the civil law of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, the civil rights of the province of Quebec were always drawn up by learned jurists and passed on by a succes-

sion of studious generations, especially devoted however, to the importance of retaining principles which we received from the French law, derived from the Paris custom.
And today, with a single pen stroke, many sections including those I mentioned are being violated.
I challenge the Minister of Public Works -who has spoken a while ago without convincing many people-and his colleagues on the other side of the house, to prove that the provisions of clause 15, as drawn up now, do not violate those sections.
In the civil code, as well as in the civil procedure code of the province of Quebec, we find very specific provisions which indicate how we should proceed to recover a debt incurred by a person under age.
And here, we turn up our noses at the protective measures issued for the good of persons under age and we pretend, by way of a simple legislative text, to translate the minority into the majority. It would be just as logical for the federal government to propose, through such a decree, that a man become a woman, or vice-versa. This is just as senseless, Mr. Chairman.
Further, I cannot understand why, after the statement made two days ago by the Minister of Justice, we do not want to follow up today the pledge taken by the federal Minister of Justice on behalf of the government.
In fact, here is what the Minister of Justice stated, as can be found on page 5775 of Hansard:
I give notice immediately that when we reach clause 15 I will move an amendment which will clarify that clause and will also quiet the fears of those who worry, with good reason in some cases...
Mr. Chairman, we must insist on those last words:
-will quiet the fears of those who worry, with good reason in some cases, about the wording of the said clause.
Mr. Chairman, we studied this measure section by section and we now are on clause 15. We are told today that there will be no amendment proposed.
I know-and the parliamentary secretary of the Minister of Justice will repeat it no doubt-that some explanation was given, but I feel it is unsatisfactory in many respects.
It is true that the opinion of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinongd-Delanau-diere was sought on the scope of this amendment, and as was to be expected, the hon. member said that the proposed amendment
Loans to Students
was inadequate. As a matter of fact, it was inadequate because it failed to remove the offensive part of clause 15. In other words, in spite of this amendment, the student under age was still considered as being of full age, which is clearly against the provisions of the civil code, which I quoted a few minutes ago, and only provided a certain protection as to procedure to follow for repayment. It was undoubtedly an inadequate amendment.
But the point I want to raise is this: If there should be any worry, and rightly so, about the interferences of this clause, it was the government's responsibility and that of the Minister of Finance in particular, to present an amendment in order to get rid of that concern which the minister himself said was found, and if the parliamentary secretary had moved an amendment we could have discussed its merits. We would have no doubt come to a satisfactory and adequate understanding to guarantee the rights of the civil code of the province of Quebec as well as those of common law of the other provinces.
The Minister of Public Works has stated, I believe, that under the Bank Act, and the Bills of Exchange Act, this was the practice. In my opinion, the minister went quite beyond the legal reality, with regard to this matter.
I could, for instance, mention section 48 of the Bills of Exchange Act, chapter 15 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, which I have here in English. I quote:

Where a bill Is drawn or endorsed by an Infant, minor, or corporation having no capacity or power to incur liability on a bill, the drawing or endorsement entitles the holder to receive payment of the bill, and to enforce it against any other party thereto.

Any party having legal capacity is bound by the bill but the minor cannot be, whereas in that clause, the minor is assimilated, purely and simply, to a person enjoying full capacity.
Before ending my remarks, I say that this provision is unconstitutional and that it would create the worst precedent possible in the field of public legislation.
Mr. Chairman, I have never seen a government care so little about such important matters. As a matter of fact, one only has to remember the careless remarks made by the parliamentary secretary when he explained why he refused to proceed now with an amendment which he had found warranted.
Mr. Chairman, it seems that it is not too late for the government to change its mind.

Loans to Students
Even if consideration of that section had to stand until tomorrow morning to allow officials of the Department of Justice to draft a proper amendment or remove clause 15 entirely, I think it would be well worthwhile. In my opinion, in the years to come it would be better to eliminate this source of dispute -and I really mean a source of dispute- because this clause is truly a nest of lawsuits since any time a minor is sued under this unconstitutional provision, he will just have to invoke provincial law to have the lawsuit thrown out of court on a technicality.
Since the clause is ill-founded, I feel the government should introduce an appropriate amendment or remove the clause entirely.
In my opinion, if members on this side of the house really wish to do their duty as members of parliament, they must insist that such a course of action be followed before the clause is passed by the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I listened closely to the remarks made by the Minister of Public Works for whom I have much sympathy. However, his observation did not convince me. I submit that this legislation is of a banking nature rather than concerning the legal capacity of minors and I do not agree with him at all. He is wrong. At that rate, the federal government could take advantage of any legislation and include a banking provision to interfere in any field at all. In such a case, we could say that the municipalities could use the Bank Act or that the banks could use the municipalities act. It is somewhat as if the federal government introduced banking legislation to help a municipality and passed an amendment to force them to hoist a union jack on the city hall. And it would be said that it came under the banks act. Come, now. The arguments he advanced sounded a little like that.
According to the argument put forward by the minister, it is true that a minor can do business with a bank each time it is to his advantage; but when it is to his disadvantage, let us say that a youth of 18 borrows $1,000 from a bank and instead of using the money to pay for his tuition he spends it to buy a car and has an accident on the highway so that the $1,000 vanish into thin air, then the civil code says clearly that the bank would

not be entitled to demand the repayment of the loan.
This is what happens-and the Minister of Public Works will agree I am sure-in the usual course of banking business. But why should a change be made under the students loans act? There would be no reason.
Now the minister says that if the amendment of the hon. member for Berthier-Mas-kinonge-Delanaudiere was passed, this would cancel the act. This is not true, because the bank would then be repaid by the minor; it might get repayment from the minor, unless it might be proved that he could not enjoy the loan.
If the minor used the loan to study, the bank will not lose anything under the guarantee of the government, and then the amendment included in the bill would not cancel at all the provisions of the bill as a whole. This is quite simple.
This would help the minors in general who would take advantage of the loan to continue their studies, but in the case of minors who would be at a disadvantage because of the loan-and this will happen-then the federal government will have to pay, under the guarantee it gives under section 7, I believe, of the bill. Section 7 has not been inserted in the bill for nothing. It is there for a purpose. That is when minors would use it.
As it stands now, however, the bill goes directly against the Quebec code of civil procedure. The Minister of Public Works should be the first one to realize it and we cannot accept that.
It is also contrary to civil procedure in other provinces. It is said that Quebec will not participate in the scheme. As far as we are concerned, we will let the other provinces vote on that. If they want to hang themselves, let them do it; indeed, that is what they have been doing for years by favouring centralization.
The other provinces are surrendering all their powers, all their jurisdictions to Ottawa. As for us, we will not participate in the program; it will not concern us. It is up to the other provinces to make up their own minds; if they want to surrender all their powers to Ottawa, if Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, British Columbia and the maritime provinces want to do that, I could not care less, it is up to them to decide, not us.
At least, in our case, we will have fought for our rights. As far as clause 15 is concerned, it will not violate our rights, but they will be violated, in principle, by clause 12.
